extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, literary critics, and men of letters (eighteenth‑century reading public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating literary works (especially pastorals) and for cultivating habits of study, conversation, and writing appropriate to a man of letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of reading, conversation, and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading makes a full man, conversation a ready man, and writing an exact man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read, converse, and write in due proportions: reading supplies knowledge, conversation supplies facility and adaptability, and writing supplies method and precision. Strive toward perfection as an ideal, even if unattainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation of predecessors and learned authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reject libraries or the writings of predecessors; consult other understandings than your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since only very few can add materially to knowledge, and much of our understanding derives from others, it is arrogant and prejudicial to dismiss earlier authors. Learning from predecessors strengthens judgment and reduces reinventing errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid solitary study at the expense of communicative skill
rubrics_metrics.description: A recluse may acquire knowledge but lose the power to teach or speak intelligibly to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solitary habit leads to expecting cramped allusions and short hints to suffice for others; to avoid being unintelligible, the studious should cultivate conversation and public exposition to learn application and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conversation to test ideas but beware sophistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation makes a man ready, but may tempt him to seize unfair advantages in argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While conversation trains adaptability, it can foster techniques that silence opponents rather than establish truth (e.g., unjust concessions, specious proofs). Beware allowing conversational victories to substitute for rigorous reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to fix thoughts: method, clarity, and detection of fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: To fix the thoughts by writing, and subject them to frequent examinations and reviews, is the best method of enabling the mind to detect its own sophisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing contracts and orders thoughts; method is the excellence of writing. Use composition to expose and remedy confusions learned in oral debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep perfection in view as a guiding standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfection should be kept in our eye, that we may always advance towards it, though we know it never can be reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for human limitations, but hold the ideal of perfection to guide continuous improvement of reading, speaking, and writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of sound literary criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic should show candour and love of truth, avoid bigotry and captiousness, and distribute praise justly between ancients and moderns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice sober deference to established reputation without blind adoration, and be willing to favour later performances without being fond of novelty for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / inventive power (in pastoral poetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether a poet is an inventor or chiefly an imitator (e.g., Theocritus as original; Virgil as imitator/rival).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value genuine invention: repeating established forms or slavish imitation lowers a poet's claim to inventive praise; compare degree of novelty against antecedent models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of diction to pastoral simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnificence of diction can conflict with the simplicity proper to pastoral poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise elevated diction where it fits the subject, but beware when splendour of style departs from the pastoral character and thereby diminishes its appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of subject and occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: The theme and tone of a poem should fit the occasion that produced it (e.g., the poem to Pollio is disproportionate to its occasion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the poet's sentiment and scale suit the event or person celebrated; an over‑grand subject for a small occasion reflects injudicious choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of affecting sentiment and pleasing description
rubrics_metrics.description: A pastoral should contain affecting sentiments and pleasing descriptions that strike the imagination and awaken the passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poem provokes genuine feeling and vivid imagery; lack of such elements (as alleged in Virgil's second pastoral) weakens its merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of pastoral innocence and dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastoral characters and situations should maintain the innocence and dignity proper to the form; coarse invective or degraded behavior is inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticize scenes that lower the pastoral tone (e.g., scurrilous quarrels) as undermining the genre's essential charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of repetitive plans or contests
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating the same contest plan in multiple pastorals suggests lack of inventive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value variety of design and fresh treatments rather than recycling the same structure (e.g., two pastorals of the same contest type attract reproach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and compositional integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem should present as a coherent, intentional composition, not an assembly of fragments or borrowed pieces (e.g., the ninth pastoral appears fragmentary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question works that feel patched together or lack discernible design; compositional unity is a mark of authentic authorship and care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of mythological imagery and natural feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Overreliance on mythological or invented images reduces the natural, rational sentiments expected in pastoral lament or praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer images and sentiments that arise from natural feeling and pastoral life; mythological ornamentation should not substitute for genuine emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and diversification within a poem
rubrics_metrics.description: A pastoral (or any poem) benefits from diversity of incident and sentiment; the first and tenth pastorals are singled out for such quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works that mix tones and scenes with greater esteem; monotony or narrow scope diminishes interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification for choice of fable or allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection of particular fables or mythic material must be suitable and defensible relative to the poem's aims (e.g., question raised about Silenus' fable choices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the chosen fables advance the poem's purpose and are congruent with its moral or thematic design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility and breadth of accomplishment (portrait of the accomplished gentleman)
rubrics_metrics.description: An admirable man of letters combines extensive learning with accomplishments in arts, music, horsemanship, fencing, memory, and public performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Versatility—skill in languages, disputation, arts, music, dancing, sport, and memory—marks exceptional merit; public demonstrations (disputations, tilting, acting) serve as proof of such breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public demonstration as proof of merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Public disputations, challenges, and performances serve to display learning and capabilities (e.g., public disputations at universities and courts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to work or character that has been tested and acclaimed in public, while recognizing that public success may be accompanied by vanity or tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical virtues: courage, generosity, and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning should be matched by martial courage, generous conduct (e.g., dividing winnings among widows), and appropriate comportment; deficiencies in these areas stain reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the moral and practical behavior of authors/figures alongside intellectual achievements; personal conduct colors the legacy of talent.
